channel.title: The Officer's Bookshelf
channel.description: Long-form conversations about books worth reading closely. Each week takes on a single title — an overview first, then chapter by chapter, then the themes still worth arguing about long after the last page.

item.title: E7 · Closing Review — SPQR
item.description: A closing conversation on SPQR as a whole: what Beard is arguing against, how well her method holds up, where the sceptical reading of the sources is most and least convincing, and what the book offers a reader who wants Rome as history rather than as fable.
item.content:encoded:
A closing conversation on SPQR: A History of Ancient Rome as a whole. We pull the threads together: incorporation as the engine of Roman power, the persistent gap between what Romans said about their past and what can be evidenced, and Beard's refusal to organise a thousand years around the biographies of great men.

We also weigh where the book strains: whether ending at 212 CE dodges questions readers come for, whether the scepticism is applied evenly, and how much a single volume can say about military and economic history while giving so much room to the social. And we ask what it is for — what a serving officer or any general reader takes from Rome told this way.
item.itunes:author: Percy Fitzwallace

item.title: E6 · Part 5: Provinces & Legacy — SPQR
item.description: Rome outside Rome: governors and garrisons, Britain to Syria, the letters of Pliny and Trajan, and the everyday business of running an empire — closing with Caracalla's edict of 212 CE, where Beard chooses to end, and why she refuses the story of decline and fall.
item.content:encoded:
The empire as experienced from the edges. Beard moves out to the provinces — soldiers' letters from Vindolanda, the correspondence between Pliny in Bithynia and the emperor Trajan, the modest staffing of vast territories — and shows how much of Roman rule depended on local elites choosing to become Roman.

She ends in 212 CE, when Caracalla granted citizenship to nearly every free person in the empire: a moment that completes the book's central theme of incorporation, and a deliberate refusal of the usual terminus of decline and fall. The episode closes on what Rome left behind and why its arguments about citizenship, empire and belonging keep resurfacing.
item.itunes:author: Percy Fitzwallace

item.title: E5 · Part 4: Emperors & Society — SPQR
item.description: The emperors from Tiberius to Commodus — and Beard's argument that the lurid biographies matter less than the machinery that kept working regardless. Alongside them, the Roman home front: family, slavery, freedmen, food, work, and the lives of the people the histories mostly ignore.
item.content:encoded:
Fourteen emperors, and a case for reading them differently. Beard sets the familiar catalogue of monsters and paragons — Caligula's horse, Nero's fiddle, the good emperors of the second century — against the striking continuity of imperial administration, and suggests the scandal stories tell us more about senatorial anxiety than about how the empire was actually run.

The other half of the episode turns away from the palace: households and marriage, the sheer scale and ordinariness of slavery, the freedmen who became rich and the epitaphs they left, the economics of bread and housing, and what tombstones, graffiti and shopping lists reveal about Romans who never appear in Tacitus.
item.itunes:author: Percy Fitzwallace

item.title: E4 · Part 3: Revolution & Augustus — SPQR
item.description: The end of the republic and the making of one-man rule: Pompey and Caesar, the civil wars and the Ides of March, and then the long, careful transformation by which Octavian became Augustus and an emperor came to look like a restored republic.
item.content:encoded:
The republic's last generation: the informal dominance of the great commanders, Cicero's consulship and the Catilinarian conspiracy, Caesar in Gaul and at the Rubicon, and the assassination that solved nothing. Beard is sharp on how contemporaries struggled to name what was happening to them, and on how much of the "fall of the republic" is hindsight.

Then the Augustan settlement — the most consequential political improvisation in Roman history. Octavian's victory at Actium, the slow accumulation of powers under republican titles, the building programme and the poetry, and the unanswered question the whole system rested on: how do you hand on a position that officially does not exist?
item.itunes:author: Percy Fitzwallace

item.title: E3 · Part 2: Expansion & Crisis — SPQR
item.description: From a middling Italian town to the dominant power of the Mediterranean: the conquest of Italy, the Punic Wars and the destruction of Carthage — and then the political crisis that success brought home, from the Gracchi through Marius and Sulla.
item.content:encoded:
How Rome grew. Beard's answer turns on something unusual: a willingness to absorb the defeated, extending citizenship and alliance rather than simply subjugating, which kept producing more Romans and more soldiers. The conquest of Italy, the wars with Carthage and Hannibal's invasion, and the absorption of the Greek east follow from there.

The second half of the episode is the bill coming due at home: land, debt and the dispossessed; the Gracchi and the turn to political violence; Marius and the professionalised army loyal to its commander; the Social War; and Sulla's march on Rome — the republic's institutions failing to scale to the empire they had won.
item.itunes:author: Percy Fitzwallace

item.title: E2 · Part 1: Origins & Kings — SPQR
item.description: The foundation stories and the regal period: Romulus and Remus, Aeneas and the Trojan inheritance, the seven kings and the expulsion of Tarquin — and Beard's careful separation of what Romans told themselves about their beginnings from what the archaeology will actually support.
item.content:encoded:
Rome's beginnings as the Romans narrated them: twins suckled by a wolf, a fratricide at the founding, the rape of the Sabine women, and the Trojan refugee Aeneas grafted on to give Rome a pedigree as old as Greece's. Beard treats these less as bad history than as evidence of how Romans understood violence, asylum and identity as built into their city from the start.

Then the regal period and its end: the seven kings, the reforms credited to them, the expulsion of Tarquin the Proud, and the founding of the republic in 509 BCE — a date and a story she shows to be far shakier than the tradition allows, set against what excavation in the Forum and on the Palatine can and cannot tell us.
item.itunes:author: Percy Fitzwallace

item.title: E1 · Overview — SPQR
item.description: Mary Beard's history of ancient Rome asks how a small and unremarkable town in central Italy came to rule an empire of some fifty million people — and why, two thousand years later, we are still arguing with the Romans. A full-book overview of her argument and method before the part-by-part episodes that follow.
item.content:encoded:
SPQR: A History of Ancient Rome (2015) is Mary Beard's account of Rome's first millennium, from the misty foundation stories to 212 CE, when the emperor Caracalla made every free inhabitant of the empire a Roman citizen. She opens not at the beginning but in 63 BCE, with Cicero against Catiline — a deliberate choice that puts evidence and argument, rather than chronology, at the centre.

This first episode takes the book whole: Beard's insistence that Rome's rise was neither inevitable nor the work of destiny, her sceptical handling of the sources, and her recurring interest in the people the traditional histories leave out — slaves, freedmen, soldiers, women, provincials.

The episodes that follow move through the book in order: origins and the kings, expansion and the crisis of the republic, the revolution that ended it and the Augustan settlement, the emperors and Roman society, and the provinces and the long legacy — closing with a full-book review.
